td_rubrique_intro: Calculators that follow the course exercises and practicals step by step, with your numbers, then show the exact calculation.
td_calc_parallaxe_aide: ISS altitude or Moon distance from two elevations taken at the same instant, as in the practical; then the exact calculation.
td_p_intro: The practical: read in Stellarium the elevations h₁ and h₂ of the object seen from both places at the same instant; the parallax is 2α = h₁ − h₂; the distance R between the two places is measured “for instance with Google Earth” or with astropy’s EarthLocation; finally 2α = R / D (2α in radians). Positions can be written in any way (48°47′6″N, 48.785, 2.45 E…).
td_conf_aide: Without azimuth, the object is assumed in the vertical plane containing both places: between them (each sees it toward the other) or on the same side (beyond the place that sees it highest). With both azimuths, this is not needed.
td_p_aide: Latitude and longitude, written in any way: 48°47′6″N 2°27′E, 48.785, 2.45, 48 47 06 N 2 27 00 E, 48d47m6s… Without letters: latitude then longitude.
td_alt_aide: Elevation of the place (m, or “1.2 km”).
td_h_aide: Elevation (altitude above the horizon) read in Stellarium; for the Moon, the Moon–star angular distance φ of the practical works too (same calculation).
td_az_aide: Azimuth read in Stellarium (north 0°, east 90°). With both azimuths, the exact calculation triangulates the lines of sight in space.
td_instant_aide: Instant of the measurement, in universal time: used to compare with the ephemeris.
td_maintenant_aide: Date and time UT of this computer.
td_sigma_t_aide: Possible offset between both measurements (seconds): multiplied by the object’s speed in elevation (from the ephemeris, if the time is given).
td_eph_etat_de440: Moon: JPL DE440 (cached file). ISS: CelesTrak TLE.
td_eph_etat_meeus: Moon: Meeus approximation (a few km); DE440 (32 MB, once) for better. ISS: CelesTrak TLE.
td_de440_aide: Reduced JPL DE440 ephemeris (de440s.bsp, 32 MB, public domain), downloaded once and kept; everything then works offline.
td_tle_recuperer_aide: ISS TLE closest to the instant: cache, otherwise CelesTrak (current elements). TLE history is not freely available without a Space-Track account: for an old pass, paste a TLE of that time.
td_tle_aide: Two TLE lines (can be typed offline).
td_tle_recu: TLE of {date} UT ({source}), {age} days from the instant.
td_calculer_aide: All the steps of the practical with your numbers, then the exact calculation.
td_exemple_aide: Fill in with consistent FICTITIOUS data (two large cities).
td_exemple_fictif: Example: fictitious data (public cities, computed elevations).
td_exporter_aide: The calculation details (CSV) for the “Calculs” sheet of the share.
td_zoom_aide: Close in the drawing around the two places (× 1 to × 60).
td_schema_aide: Cross-section of the Earth in the plane of both places: chord R, verticals (dashed), horizons (green), lines of sight (red), angles; magnifier: the sagitta between the chord and the surface.
td_schema_vide: Enter both places and both elevations, then “Calculate” (or “Example”).
td_detail_aide: The steps of the practical, numbered, with your numbers.
td_e2_entre: The object is BETWEEN the two places: the lines of sight cross above the baseline, and the practical’s formula (a difference) becomes 2α = 180° − h₁ − h₂ = {a}° = {r} rad.
td_e3_t: At the surface (like Google Earth): {s} km. In a straight line (chord, astropy EarthLocation, WGS84): {c} km, {e} m shorter. The chord runs below the ground: sagitta of {f} m at the middle (≈ R²/(8 R⊕) = {fa} m); it dips {p1}° and {p2}° below the horizon of each place.
td_e4_t: D = {c} km / {a} rad = {dc} km (with the chord); {ds} km with the surface distance.
td_e5_t: The two horizons are not parallel: they make {theta}° between them (angle at the Earth’s centre). Triangulation of the lines of sight ({mode}): distances {d1} km and {d2} km, distance to the Earth’s centre {dg} km, altitude {alt} km; angle between the lines of sight {p}°.
td_mode_entre: object between the places, in their vertical plane
td_mode_meme_cote: object on the same side, in the places’ vertical plane
td_e6_lune: Moon ({src}): {dg} km from the Earth’s centre, {d1} km and {d2} km from the places; predicted elevations {h1}° and {h2}° without refraction ({hr1}° and {hr2}° with).
td_e6_iss: ISS (TLE {age} days away): altitude {alt} km, {d1} km and {d2} km from the places; predicted elevations {h1}° and {h2}°.
td_e7_t: With σ(h) = {sh}° (time included) and the places’ uncertainty: D (practical) to ± {s} km, exact distance to ± {x} km.
td_a_inversion_certaine: Place {n}: latitude and longitude swapped (latitude > 90°), corrected.
td_a_inversion_probable: Place {n}: latitude and longitude probably swapped (the baseline would become reasonable). Check.
td_a_inversion_un_des_deux: Huge baseline: latitude and longitude probably swapped for one of the two places. Check.
td_a_tle_ancien: The TLE is {j} days from the instant: approximate ISS prediction (several km).
td_a_lune_azimuts: Moon without azimuths: the Moon is generally not in the vertical plane of both places; give the azimuths for an exact calculation.
td_err_signe: “{texte}”: sign and letter contradict each other.
td_err_deux_angles: “{texte}”: two angles are needed, latitude and longitude.
td_err_parallaxe_nulle: Zero parallax: both elevations are equal.
td_err_meme_lieu: The two places are the same.
td_err_derriere: The lines of sight do not cross in front of the observers (check the elevations, azimuths or object position).
td_err_tle: TLE unreadable or outside its validity.
td_aide_html:
Course calculators

Each calculator follows the approach of an exercise or practical of the course, step by step, with YOUR numbers, then shows the exact calculation and what changes.

Parallax (course practical)

  1. Readings: elevations h₁ and h₂ of the ISS (or of the Moon) at the same instant from two places, read in Stellarium (and, if possible, the azimuths).
  2. Parallax: 2α = h₁ − h₂ (object seen on the same side); if the object is BETWEEN the places, the lines of sight cross and 2α = 180° − h₁ − h₂.
  3. Distance R between the places: at the surface (Google Earth) or in a straight line (the chord, astropy EarthLocation). The chord runs below the ground: its sagitta is ≈ R²/(8 R⊕), 3 km for 400 km.
  4. D = R / 2α, 2α in radians.

The exact calculation accounts for curvature: the two horizons make the angle θ at the Earth’s centre (4.5° for 500 km). For the Moon, the difference h₁ − h₂ is almost entirely due to θ: the practical’s formula applied to elevations gives thousands of km instead of 380,000; that is why the Moon practical measures the Moon–star distance. With azimuths, the lines of sight are triangulated in space; otherwise the object is assumed in the vertical plane of both places.

With the time: ephemeris (Moon: JPL DE440 downloaded once, otherwise Meeus; ISS: CelesTrak TLE, TLE history not being freely available) and predicted elevations to compare. Propagated uncertainties (elevations, places, time). Refraction (≈ 34′ at the horizon) and the thickness of air crossed are explained by the “Earth’s atmosphere” animation (Telescopes theme). “Example”: fictitious data. “Export the details”: for the “Calculs” sheet of the share.
